one_liner: Training-free block-sparse, INT8/FP8-quantized attention kernels; 1.8-4.5x per-layer over full attention in model runs, approximate.
what_it_does: A PyTorch CUDA extension that replaces torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention in inference with an approximate attention that predicts and skips negligible 128x64 blocks of the attention map. The recommended call is spas_sage2_attn_meansim_topk_cuda(q, k, v, topk=0.5, is_causal=False), where topk is the fraction of key blocks kept per query block; block_sparse_sage2_attn_cuda takes your own per-head 0/1 block mask. It works without retraining or (in the current API) per-model tuning, and is forward-only.
how_it_is_fast: Two multipliers stack: sparsity and SageAttention-style quantization. A Triton pre-pass mean-pools each Q and K block, keeps blocks whose tokens are not self-similar, scores the pooled blocks with a softmax and keeps the top-k fraction (or a CDF threshold) of key blocks, producing a lookup table the kernel walks. The CUDA kernels quantize Q and K to INT8 (K mean-smoothed) and, on sm89/sm90, V to FP8 with FP16 or FP32 accumulation (SageAttention2/2++), and a pv_threshold variant skips further P·V work inside the kernel.
when_to_use: Inference of video and image diffusion transformers (CogVideoX, Mochi, Wan, Flux, SD3.5) at long token counts (17K-22K and up), where Table 1 shows 3.1-3.5x per-layer attention speedups with near-dense quality metrics.
Long-context LLM prefill (Llama3.1 at 128K in Table 1, about 4.5x per layer) when a small accuracy loss is acceptable and you use non-causal attention or the SageAttention1-based API (see gotchas).
Ampere, Ada or Hopper GPUs (A100, RTX 4090, H100/H20) with head dim 64 or 128 and FP16/BF16 activations.
You already have a per-head block-sparse pattern (sliding tiles, video-locality masks) and want a fast INT8/FP8 kernel that executes it via block_sparse_sage2_attn_cuda.
when_not_to_use: Training or fine-tuning: there is no backward pass or autograd function.
Workloads that need exact attention, or causal attention through the recommended SageAttention2-based APIs (see gotchas).

Short sequences: at 4.5K tokens (Flux, SD3.5) the gain is only about 1.8x, sequences under 128 tokens are rejected, and at low sparsity the FlashAttention2-based variant is only about 1.1x over FlashAttention2 in Figure 2.

Blackwell GPUs or new toolchains: setup.py lists only compute capabilities 8.0, 8.6, 8.7, 8.9 and 9.0, issue #109 (open, no reply) reports the build rejecting TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0 on an RTX 5090, and issues #115/#122/#114 report build failures with CUDA 13.0, GCC 13+ and Python 3.14.
Head dims other than 64 or 128 (you must pad and pass the softmax scale yourself).

integration.dependencies: PyTorch>=2.3, Triton (block-map kernels), einops; ninja for the build; CUDA toolkit with nvcc
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 and CUDA 12.0+ (12.4+ for sm89/sm90, 12.8+ for the SageAttention2++ FP16-accumulate path), Python 3.9+; built from source with setup.py (no wheel documented)
integration.platforms: Linux, NVIDIA sm80/sm86/sm87 (INT8 QK, FP16 PV), sm89 and sm90a (INT8 QK, FP8 PV); Blackwell not in setup.py's supported list; Windows source builds reported failing at link time (issue #103)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; every call runs torch.cuda.set_device(v.device), changing the caller's current device, and issue #97 (open) reports that calling it twice can corrupt the CUDA context
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same (q, k, v, is_causal) call shape as torch SDPA, but the default layout is HND, head dim must be 64 or 128, attn_mask and dropout_p are accepted and ignored, there is no backward, and the output is an approximation controlled by topk

gotchas: Causal masking in the recommended APIs: spas_sage2_attn_meansim_topk_cuda (and the other SageAttention2-based entry points) builds a causal block map but launches the kernel with the causal flag hard-coded to False, so the diagonal blocks run unmasked and a query can see up to 127 later tokens in its block (from reading spas_sage_attn/core.py and utils.py, not tested). The SageAttention1-based spas_sage_attn_meansim_topk_cuda passes is_causal through to the kernel.
Silent dtype changes: output_dtype is ignored (the output takes the input dtype), and for BF16 inputs V is cast to FP16, which overflows for |v| above 65504.

Open correctness reports against the recommended API: random black output (#110), garbled results (#106), and undefined values in masked tail loads of the block-pooling kernels when the sequence is not a multiple of the block size (#124, fix proposed in PR #125).

The entry points are decorated with @torch.compiler.disable, so torch.compile graphs break around every attention call; the published Table 1 numbers came from the older SageAttention1-based version, and the README says the SageAttention2-based one is about 30% faster.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over SageAttention when sequences are long and attention maps are sparse: it reuses the same INT8/FP8 kernels and adds block skipping (SageAttention alone is about 300 vs FlashAttention2's 165 TOPS in Figure 2, SpargeAttn+Sage2 up to about 875). Prefer FlashAttention-3/4 when you need exact attention, a backward pass, or causal LLM training, and Chipmunk if you specifically want column-sparse attention for diffusion transformers measured against FlashAttention-3.
verified_claims_summary: README Figure 2 (RTX 4090, sequence 22K, head dim 128) plots kernel TOPS against sparsity: FlashAttention2 about 165, SageAttention about 300, SpargeAttn+Sage2 about 410 at sparsity 0.1 rising to about 875 at 0.6 (about 2.5-5.3x, chart readings, derived from page data). Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png, GPU not stated, older SageAttention1-based version) gives per-layer attention speed in real model runs of 1.8x (Flux, SD3.5 at 4.5K) to 4.5x (Llama3.1 at 128K) over full attention with near-dense accuracy; no compiler flags or kernel benchmark script are published.
status_note: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE and source headers; setup.py metadata says BSD 3-Clause) and copyable, but the last commit was 2026-02-25 and 62 issues are open, including unanswered build failures on CUDA 13, GCC 13 and Blackwell, so treat it as research code with slowing maintenance.
